title: Fair games and martingales
objectives: Recognise a martingale by checking that its expected next value, given the history, equals its value now.

screens.title: A fair bet
screens.prose: You start with £10 and bet £1 on each toss of a fair coin. Heads wins £1 and tails loses £1. The chart shows 20 such bankrolls and the dashed mean line.
screens.question: After 8 tosses your bankroll is £13. What do you expect it to be after toss 9, and after toss 18?

hints.text: After toss 9 you hold £14 or £12, each with chance one half.
Average the two: $\tfrac12(14 + 12)$. Each later toss is just as fair.
Both forecasts are £13: a fair toss adds nothing on average, however far ahead you look.

feedback.correct: £13 both times. A fair bet does not move the forecast.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the two possible bankrolls after one toss, then ask what each later toss adds.

byKey.r0c1: Check toss 9. You hold £14 or £12 with equal chance, and the start of £10 no longer matters.
byKey.r1c1: Check toss 18. Each of the 10 tosses is as likely to lose £1 as to win it.

explain.text: After toss 9 you hold £14 or £12 with equal chance, so £13 on average. Every later toss adds 0 on average, so the forecast for toss 18 is £13 too. The dashed mean line is flat for the same reason.

screens.title: A biased coin
screens.prose: Now bias the coin. Slide the chance of heads $p$ and watch the dashed mean line. Press New paths for a fresh batch.
screens.question: With $p = 0.6$ and £13 after toss 8, what is your expected bankroll after toss 9?

hints.text: You hold £14 with chance 0.6 and £12 with chance 0.4.
Weight each bankroll by its chance: $0.6 \times 14 + 0.4 \times 12$.

feedback.correct: £13.20: each toss now gains $0.6 - 0.4 = 0.2$ on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight £14 by 0.6 and £12 by 0.4.

byKey.fair: That is the fair answer. With $p = 0.6$ each toss gains $0.6 - 0.4 = 0.2$ on average.
byKey.gains: You added the expected win, £0.60, but forgot the expected loss: £1 with chance 0.4.
byKey.win: £14 is the result after heads. Tails still happens with chance 0.4.

explain.text: $0.6 \times 14 + 0.4 \times 12 = 13.2$. Each toss now adds $2p - 1 = 0.2$ on average, so the mean line tilts upwards. The forecast is no longer today's value.

screens.title: Martingales
screens.prose: The fair bankroll has a special property: whatever has happened, its expected next value is its value now. Such a process is a **martingale**: $$E[X_{n+1} \mid X_0, \dots, X_n] = X_n \text{ for every } n,$$ with $E|X_n|$ finite. We condition on the whole history, everything seen so far.
screens.question: Each process below uses fair coin tosses. Which one is a martingale?

options.text: The number of heads so far
options.why: You saw that it never falls. It rises by $\tfrac12$ a toss on average, so its forecast is above its value.
The best so far can only stay put or rise. Its forecast is above today's value when a new high is possible.

options.text: Your bankroll when the casino keeps 5p of every £1 win
options.why: Each toss now adds $0.5 \times 0.95 - 0.5 = -0.025$ on average, so the forecast falls.

hints.text: For each process, ask what the next value is on average, given today's value.
A martingale's forecast equals its present value exactly.
Only the fair bankroll adds 0 on average. The others drift up or down.

feedback.correct: The fair bankroll. Its forecast is always today's value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the process whose expected next value equals its value now.

byKey.heads: The heads count gains $\tfrac12$ a toss on average, so it is not a fair game.
byKey.best: The best so far can never fall, so on average it rises.
byKey.rake: The 5p charge makes each toss lose 2.5p on average.

explain.text: The fair bankroll's next value is today's plus a fair step, so its forecast is today's value. The heads count gains $\tfrac12$ a toss on average, and the best so far can only rise. The raked bankroll falls by 2.5p a toss on average.

screens.title: Subtract the drift
screens.prose: Back to $p = 0.6$, now from 0: the walk $S_n$ gains $2p - 1 = 0.2$ a step on average. Subtract that drift: $M_n = S_n - 0.2n$. The lower panel draws $M_n$ for every path.
screens.question: After 10 steps, $S_{10} = 5$. What is $E[M_{11} \mid \text{history}]$?

hints.text: First forecast $S_{11}$: one step from 5 gains 0.2 on average.
$E[S_{11} \mid \text{history}] = 5.2$. Now subtract $0.2 \times 11$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Forecast $S_{11}$, then subtract $0.2 \times 11$.

byKey.stay: You forecast $S_{11} = 5$ and then forgot $M$. $S$ gains 0.2 a step, and $M$ subtracts $0.2n$.
byKey.nodrift: 5.2 is the forecast of $S_{11}$. $M_{11}$ subtracts $0.2 \times 11 = 2.2$ from it.
byKey.ten: You subtracted $0.2 \times 10$. At step 11 the drift so far is $0.2 \times 11 = 2.2$.

explain.text: $E[S_{11} \mid \text{history}] = 5.2$, and $0.2 \times 11 = 2.2$, so the forecast of $M_{11}$ is 3. That equals $M_{10} = 5 - 2 = 3$. Subtracting the drift turns any walk into a martingale.

screens.title: A fair price
screens.prose: A share at £100 moves up 25% or down 20% each day, as in Price paths. Call the up chance $p$. For the price to be a fair game, tomorrow's expected price must be £100.
screens.question: Which up chance $p$ makes the price a martingale? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Write tomorrow's expected price in terms of $p$.

byKey.half: You took a fair coin. The moves differ in size: $0.5 \times 125 + 0.5 \times 80 = 102.5$, which drifts up.
byKey.swap: $\tfrac59$ is the down chance. The up move is the larger one, so it needs the smaller chance.
byKey.down: 0.8 is the down factor, not a chance.

explain.text: $125p + 80(1 - p) = 100$ gives $45p = 20$, so $p = \tfrac49 \approx 0.4444$. Under this chance every price on the tree is a fair game. Pricing with Trees (topic 1.7) calls it the risk-neutral chance.

screens.title: A forecaster
screens.prose: A forecaster quotes the chance of at least two heads in three fair tosses. Before any toss she says $\tfrac12$. After each toss she updates her chance. Fill in her forecasts.
screens.question: What does she quote after each of these starts?

hints.text: After one head she needs at least one more head in two tosses.
After H: $1 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac34$. After T she needs both: $\tfrac14$.
After HH she has won: 1. After HT or TH she needs one head in one toss: $\tfrac12$. After TT: 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After each start, count the heads still needed and the tosses left.

byKey.r0c1: Check the forecast after H. After a head she needs only one more head in two tosses.
byKey.r1c1: Check the forecast after T. After a tail she needs heads on both tosses left.

explain.text: Each pair averages to the forecast before it: $\tfrac12(\tfrac34 + \tfrac14) = \tfrac12$ and $\tfrac12(1 + \tfrac12) = \tfrac34$. A forecast that uses all the information so far is always a martingale. If it were expected to rise, she would raise it now.

screens.title: Unfair games
screens.prose: Most bets are not fair. A process that falls on average, $E[X_{n+1} \mid \text{history}] \le X_n$, is a **supermartingale**. One that rises on average is a **submartingale**. A European wheel has 18 red pockets out of 37.
screens.question: You bet £1 on red every spin. What is your expected change in winnings per spin? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: You win £1 with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$. What happens otherwise?
You lose £1 with chance $\tfrac{19}{37}$.

byKey.fair: You treated red as an even chance. The green zero gives the casino one extra pocket.
byKey.double: You counted the edge twice. The gap between $\tfrac{19}{37}$ and $\tfrac{18}{37}$ is $\tfrac{1}{37}$.
byKey.chance: 0.486 is the chance of red, not the expected change in pounds.

explain.text: You win £1 with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$ and lose £1 with chance $\tfrac{19}{37}$, so each spin loses $\tfrac{1}{37} \approx$ £0.027 on average. Your winnings are a supermartingale, and the mean line slopes down. The casino's takings, the mirror image, are a submartingale.

screens.title: A constant mean
screens.prose: Toss a fair coin once to set $X_0 = +1$ or $-1$. After that, $X_{n+1} = -X_n$: the process flips sign every step. Each $X_n$ is $\pm 1$ with equal chance, so $E[X_n] = 0$ for every $n$.
screens.question: Is $X_n$ a martingale?

options.text: Yes: its mean is 0 at every step
options.why: You checked only the overall mean. A martingale needs the forecast given the history to equal today's value.

options.text: No: given $X_n$, the next value is $-X_n$
Yes: each value is a fair coin
options.why: Each value alone is fair, but they are tied. Once you see $X_n$ you know $X_{n+1}$ exactly.

options.text: No, because after the first toss nothing is random
options.why: A martingale may be predictable: a constant is one. What fails is that the forecast $-X_n$ is not $X_n$.

hints.text: Suppose you see $X_5 = 1$. What do you expect $X_6$ to be?
$X_6 = -1$ for certain.
So $E[X_6 \mid X_5 = 1] = -1 \ne 1$. The defining equation fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test the forecast given the history, not the overall mean.

byKey.mean: You checked the mean. It is 0 at every step, yet given $X_n = 1$ the next value is surely $-1$.
byKey.coin: Each value is fair alone, but the next value is fixed by the last one.
byKey.fixed: Being predictable is not the problem. The prediction $-X_n$ differs from $X_n$.

explain.text: Given $X_n = 1$ the next value is $-1$ for certain, so $E[X_{n+1} \mid X_n] = -X_n \ne X_n$. A constant mean is necessary for a martingale but not enough. The test is the forecast from every possible history.

screens.title: The Pólya urn
screens.prose: An urn holds one red and one blue ball. Draw one, then return it with another of its colour. The red share starts at $\tfrac12$. After the first draw it is $\tfrac23$ or $\tfrac13$.
screens.question: The first draw was red, so the share is $\tfrac23$. What is the expected red share after the second draw?

hints.text: After a red draw the urn holds two red and one blue.
Red comes next with chance $\tfrac23$ (share $\tfrac34$), blue with $\tfrac13$ (share $\tfrac12$).
$\tfrac23 \times \tfrac34 + \tfrac13 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac23$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac23$, today's share: the red share is a martingale.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the shares $\tfrac34$ and $\tfrac12$ by their chances given a red first draw.

byKey.again: $\tfrac34$ is the share if red comes again. Blue still comes with chance $\tfrac13$.
byKey.start: You went back to the start. Given the red first draw, the urn is now two red and one blue.
byKey.equal: You weighted the two draws equally. Red is now drawn with chance $\tfrac23$.

explain.text: $\tfrac23 \times \tfrac34 + \tfrac13 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac23$, today's share. A red draw makes the next red likelier, so the steps are dependent, yet the share is a martingale. After three draws it is $\tfrac15, \tfrac25, \tfrac35$ or $\tfrac45$ with chance $\tfrac14$ each, still mean $\tfrac12$.

screens.title: A martingale keeps its mean
screens.prose: Every martingale keeps its starting mean, whatever its steps look like. We prove $E[X_n] = E[X_0]$ with the law of total expectation from Averaging averages.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, and leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Average over histories (law of total expectation): $E[X_{n+1}] = E\big[E[X_{n+1} \mid X_0, \dots, X_n]\big]$.
The martingale property replaces the inner forecast by $X_n$, so $E[X_{n+1}] = E[X_n]$.
Apply this for $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$: $E[X_1] = E[X_0]$, then $E[X_2] = E[X_1]$, and so on.
By induction $E[X_n] = E[X_0]$ for every $n$: from £10, the expected fair bankroll is £10 at every toss.
The steps are independent with mean 0, so their means add up to 0.
lines.why: Independence is not needed, and the Pólya urn does not have it. The proof uses only the forecast.

hints.text: Start by writing the mean as an average of forecasts.
The martingale property is used on the inner forecast, so it comes second.
Total expectation, the martingale property, repeat the step, conclude. Leave out the independence line.

feedback.correct: Total expectation, then the martingale property, then induction: $E[X_n] = E[X_0]$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the law of total expectation and finish with the induction.

byKey.e: That line assumes independent steps. The Pólya urn keeps its mean without them.
byKey.left-out: A line that belongs is in the Left out list. Only the independence line should be there.

explain.text: Averaging the forecast over all histories gives the mean, and the forecast is $X_n$. So the mean never changes from one step to the next. Only the forecast matters, not how the steps depend on each other.

screens.title: Check a chain
screens.prose: A Markov chain on numbers is a martingale when, from every state, the expected next state is the state itself. Write `next_mean(moves)` for one state's moves, then `is_martingale(chain)` for a whole chain. Work exactly with `Fraction`.

state.caption: The fair walk on 0 to 4 with absorbing ends, each move with chance ½: the first test chain.

screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction

def next_mean(moves):
    """Expected next value, exactly.
    moves: a list of (probability, next_value) pairs."""
    ...

def is_martingale(chain):
    """chain: a dict from each state to its list of moves.
    True when every state's next mean equals the state."""
    ...

tests.setup: tree = {Fraction(1, 2): [(Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(3, 4)), (Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(1, 4))], Fraction(3, 4): [(Fraction(1, 2), 1), (Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(1, 2))], Fraction(1, 4): [(Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(1, 2)), (Fraction(1, 2), 0)]}

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: three exact means, then six chains. The chains: a fair walk, a biased walk, the share price twice, the forecaster and the sign flip.

hints.text: `next_mean` is a weighted sum: each next value times its probability.
Compare each state with `next_mean` of its moves, for every state in the dict.
`return sum(Fraction(p) * Fraction(v) for p, v in moves)` and `return all(next_mean(m) == s for s, m in chain.items())`.

feedback.correct: Both functions pass: exact forecasts, and a check over every state.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Return a `Fraction` from `next_mean`, and test every state in `is_martingale`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that both `...` lines are replaced with return statements.

explain.text: `next_mean` is the expected next value. `is_martingale` asks every state for its forecast, so one unfair state is enough to fail. The biased walk fails at every inner state, and the sign flip fails at both.

screens.title: A binary contract
screens.prose: A contract pays £100 if the Bank of England cuts rates next month, and £0 if not. It trades at £40. Tomorrow's inflation figure is high with chance 0.6 and low with chance 0.4. After a low figure the price will be £70.
screens.question: If the price is a fair game, where must it trade after a high figure?

hints.text: Today's price must equal tomorrow's expected price.

byKey.mirror: You moved it down £30, as far as it moves up. The likelier move must be the smaller one: $0.6 \times 20$ balances $0.4 \times 30$.
byKey.stay: If it stayed at £40 after a high figure, the average tomorrow would be £52. Buyers would bid it up today.
byKey.half: £30 gives an average of £46, above today's £40.

explain.text: Fairness needs $0.6x + 0.4 \times 70 = 40$, so $x = 20$. The price of a binary contract is the market's forecast of the event, a martingale like our forecaster's. A trading signal is the claim that $E[\text{next price} \mid \text{what you know}]$ differs from today's price.

ideas: A martingale is a fair game: given everything seen so far, its expected next value is its value now.
A martingale keeps its mean, $E[X_n] = E[X_0]$, by the law of total expectation. Its steps need not be independent: the Pólya urn is one.
Subtracting the drift makes a walk fair. A forecast of revealed information is fair when the quantity has a finite mean. A price is fair under the chance that balances its moves.

formula.name: Martingale
formula.note: Falls on average: supermartingale. Rises on average: submartingale.

summary.trap: A constant mean is not enough. The forecast from every history must equal today's value.

quiz.prose: A process has $E[X_{n+1} \mid \text{history}] = X_n + 0.5$ for every $n$.
quiz.question: What kind of process is it?

options.why: A supermartingale falls on average. This one gains 0.5 a step.
A martingale's forecast equals today's value. Here the forecast is 0.5 higher.

options.text: None of these, as the steps may be dependent
options.why: The definitions use only the forecast, whatever the dependence.

feedback.correct: A submartingale: it rises by 0.5 a step on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the forecast with today's value.

byKey.super: You swapped the names. Super falls, sub rises.

explain.text: The forecast is above today's value, so the process rises on average: a submartingale. Subtracting $0.5n$ would give a martingale.

byKey.zero: A martingale keeps its starting mean, which is 7 here, not 0.
byKey.add: You added one per step. A martingale's steps add 0 on average.

explain.text: Total expectation and the martingale property give $E[X_{n+1}] = E[X_n]$ at every step. So $E[X_{20}] = E[X_0] = 7$.

quiz.prose: A share is £50. Tomorrow it is £60 with chance $p$, and £45 otherwise.
quiz.question: Which $p$ makes the price a martingale? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.half: A fair coin gives $52.50$: the up move of £10 is larger than the down move of £5.
byKey.swap: $\tfrac23$ is the down chance. The larger move needs the smaller chance.

explain.text: $45 + 15p = 50$ gives $p = \tfrac13$. The up move is twice the down move, so it needs half the chance.

quiz.prose: Given $X_n = 2$, the next value $X_{n+1}$ is 3 with chance 0.5, 1 with chance 0.3, and $x$ with chance 0.2.
quiz.question: Which $x$ makes this step fair?

byKey.two: With $x = 2$ the forecast is $1.5 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 2.2$, above today's 2.
byKey.five: You may have dropped the chances. Weight each value by its chance first.

explain.text: $0.5 \times 3 + 0.3 \times 1 = 1.8$, so $0.2x = 0.2$ and $x = 1$. Then the forecast is exactly today's 2.
